Jab judges panel aapka project dekhega, toh unhe ek standard CRUD web app ya inventory management system nahi dikhega. Unhe ek **National Security Grade Cyber Weapon** dikhega. Is level ka project aapki team ko baki general webdevelopment teams se automatically ek alag (higher) league mein daal deta hai.

Agar aap AI aur Graph visualization wala part successfully show kar dete hain, toh aapka competition waise hi eliminate ho jayega. 

**3. Brawn vs. Brain (Kyun hum Analysis par focus kar rahe hain, Scraping par nahi)** Hum apna 80% focus AI (Stylometry) aur Graph Database par isliye daal rahe hain kyunki dark web se data nikalna (scraping) aasan hai—woh majdoori (brawn) hai. what is the perspective for fisibility and viability 

When you are pitching this project to the SIH judges, **Feasibility** (Can we practically build this?) and **Viability** (Is it actually useful, sustainable, and better than existing options?) will be their biggest criteria. 

Here is exactly how you should frame the perspective for both: 

# **1. FEASIBILITY (Technical Execution: "Can we build it?")** 

Judges often doubt if students can build a "Dark Web AI Tool" in 36 hours. You must show them a highly pragmatic, risk-mitigated engineering approach. 

- **Data Feasibility (The Smart MVP):** 

   - Risk: Live Tor scraping is slow, unstable, and often blocked by hackathon Wi-Fi networks. 

   - Feasible Approach: We are not relying on live Tor connections for the core demo. We will use **offline, open-source research datasets** (like the AZSecure Dark Web Forum Dataset or archived breached forums) to simulate the data pipeline. This guarantees a zero-fail, smooth demo. 

- **AI Stylometry Feasibility:** 

   - Risk: Training a massive AI model from scratch is impossible in 36 hours. 

   - Feasible Approach: We are using pre-trained lightweight Transformer models (like **RoBERTa** or **SentenceTransformers** ) and simply finetuning them for text similarity/authorship verification. This is computationally light and can run on a standard laptop GPU or a free Google Colab instance. 

- **Architecture Feasibility:** 

   - The core stack (Python/FastAPI, React, Neo4j) relies entirely on welldocumented, open-source technologies. Generating relationship graphs using Neo4j's Cypher queries and visualizing them with React libraries (like react-force-graph or Cytoscape.js) is a standard, highly achievable engineering task. 

- **Infrastructure Scanning Feasibility:** 

   - Finding misconfigurations doesn't require zero-day exploits. It just requires automating simple Python scripts (OpenSSL wrappers, HTTP banner grabbing) and querying the **Shodan API** (which has a free student tier). 

# **2. VIABILITY (Real-World Value: "Will NTRO actually use this?")** 

This is where you prove that your solution makes sense in the real world compared to expensive alternatives. 

#  **Strategic Sovereignty (The Biggest Selling Point):** 

- Currently, agencies use foreign tools like Maltego or DarkOwl. Passing sensitive Indian intelligence queries through foreign servers is a massive national security risk. Our solution is **100% sovereign (Made in India)** , meaning it can be deployed on NTRO’s private, air-gapped servers with zero data leakage. 

#  **Cost & Resource Efficiency:** 

   - Commercial threat intelligence licenses cost hundreds of thousands of dollars annually per agency. Our solution is built on open-source frameworks, bringing the software licensing cost down to zero. The only costs are cloud compute and Shodan API access. 

- **Operational Viability (Workflow Integration):** 

   - Analysts currently suffer from "alert fatigue" and tool fragmentation (using 5 different tools for one investigation). Our dashboard is highly viable because it consolidates Infrastructure, Financials (Crypto), and Human Behavior (AI Stylometry) into **one single visual plane** . It reduces a 2-week investigation down to a 2-minute query. 

- **Scalability for the Future:** 

- Because the architecture uses Microservices (Kafka for data ingestion, FastAPI for backend, Neo4j for graphing), it is horizontally scalable. In production, NTRO can simply add more Tor proxy nodes to increase scraping speed without rewriting the core software. 

**How to summarize this for the Judges (The Pitch):** 

"Respected Judges, from a **Feasibility** standpoint, we have de-risked the technical challenges by using pre-trained Transformer models and simulated data pipelines for the MVP, ensuring a flawless demonstration. From a **Viability** standpoint, this is not just a hackathon project—it is a sovereign, open-source alternative to expensive foreign intelligence tools. It guarantees data localization for NTRO, eliminates licensing costs, and scales horizontally." 

Does your team have a plan on how you will split these tasks (Frontend, Backend, AI, Data/Security) among your members? 

hum jo bana rahe hain uski security kaise maximize kar saktein hai koi carack nahi kar sakte hain uski security kaise badhayen jissese isko koi crak na kar paye 

Sabse pehle ek cybersecurity reality check: "100% uncrackable" jaisi koi cheez nahi hoti. Lekin hum is system ko itna secure zarur bana sakte hain ki duniya ke best hackers ke liye bhi isme ghusna practically impossible ho jaye. Is approach ko **"Defense in Depth"** (Multi-layered security) kehte hain. 

Kyunki aapka system seedha Dark Web hackers ke data ko scrape aur process karega, aapka threat model normal web apps se bahut alag aur dangerous hai. Apne system ki security maximize karne ke liye aapko in 5 layers par kaam karna hoga: 

**1. OpSec (Operational Security) — Scraper ki Identity Chupana** Hackers dark web forums par traps (honeytokens) lagate hain taaki unhe scrape karne walon ka real IP address pata chal jaye. 

- **Proxy Chaining:** Aapka scraper kabhi bhi seedha internet se connect nahi hona chahiye. Hamesha Tor network aur multiple proxy layers (rotating proxies) ke through traffic bhejen. 

- **DNS Leak Protection:** Ensure karein ki aapke scrapers Tor ka hi DNS use kar rahe hain, warna ISP ko pata chal jayega ki aapka server dark web access kar raha hai. 

- **Headless Browser Hardening:** Agar aap Selenium/Puppeteer use kar rahe hain, toh uske "webdriver" flags hide karein, warna target site detect kar legi ki ye ek bot hai. 

**2. Data Sanitization (The "Poisoned Data" Defense)** Ye sabse critical point hai. Aap jin hackers ko track kar rahe hain, wo apne forum posts ya usernames mein malicious code (SQL Injection, XSS payloads, ya Zip bombs) likh kar chhod sakte hain. 

   - **Strict Input Validation:** Jab aapka scraper dark web se text uthaye, toh use seedha database mein save na karein. Us text ko sanitize karein (HTML tags strip karein, special characters escape karein). 

   - **Zero-Trust Parsing:** Agar system dark web se koi image ya file (jaise SSL cert) download kar raha hai, toh use execute hone ki permission kabhi na dein. Use isolated environment mein parse karein. 

**3. Infrastructure & Deployment Security** Aapka code kahan run ho raha hai, ye bahut matter karta hai. 

   - **Docker Container Isolation:** Har component (Scraper, Database, AI Model, Frontend) alag-alag Docker containers mein hona chahiye. Agar hacker galti se Scraper ko hack kar bhi le, toh wo Database tak nahi pahunch payega kyunki containers isolated hain. 

   - **Air-Gapped Capability:** NTRO jaisi agencies ke liye, aapka architecture aisa hona chahiye jo internet se completely disconnect hokar (Air-gapped mode mein) local server par run kar sake. 

**4. Database & Data Security (At Rest & In Transit)** Intelligence data highly classified hota hai. 

   - **AES-256 Encryption:** Aapka Neo4j (Graph) aur PostgreSQL database hard drive par encrypted hona chahiye. 

   - **TLS 1.3:** Frontend (React) aur Backend (FastAPI) ke beech jitna bhi data travel kare, wo end-to-end encrypted hona chahiye. 

   - **Environment Variables:** API keys (jaise Shodan ki key) ya database passwords kabhi bhi code/GitHub mein hardcode nahi hone chahiye. Inhe .env files ya AWS Secrets Manager jaisi jagah store karein. 

**5. Access Control (IAM - Identity & Access Management)** Agar system hack nahi ho sakta, toh hackers authorized user ka account churane ki koshish karenge. 

   - **Strict Role-Based Access Control (RBAC):** Har user ko sirf utna hi access dein jitni uski zarurat hai. Ek 'Junior Analyst' database delete nahi kar paana chahiye. 

   - **Mandatory 2FA/MFA:** Bina OTP ya hardware token (YubiKey) ke kisi bhi analyst ko dashboard par login na karne dein. 

   - **Audit Logging:** Backend mein ek log maintain karein ki "Kis user ne, kis IP se, kitne baje, konsa threat actor search kiya". Agar koi insider threat (gaddar) data churanne ki koshish kare, toh log mein pakda jayega.

# **1. Analysis of the Feasibility of the Idea** 

**Technical Feasibility:** Building this system within a hackathon timeframe is highly feasible because we are not reinventing the wheel; we are integrating powerful opensource technologies. 

- **AI Stylometry:** We do not need to train a massive AI model from scratch. We can fine-tune pre-trained open-source NLP models (like RoBERTa or SentenceTransformers) specifically for authorship verification. 

- **Infrastructure Scanning:** Automating Tor .onion resolution and grabbing SSL certificates requires standard Python networking libraries (like requests via Tor proxies and ssl). Correlating this with clearnet IPs is easily done using the **Shodan API** , which provides a developer tier. 

- **Relationship Mapping: Neo4j** is an enterprise-grade graph database that uses the intuitive Cypher query language. It is specifically designed to handle the exact "Entity A -> connected to -> Entity B" logic the PS demands. 

**Operational Feasibility (The MVP Scope):** Instead of trying to build a crawler that indexes the entire Dark Web (which takes months and massive server farms), our MVP is highly feasible because we will focus on an **Analysis Engine** . We will use a targeted subset of data (simulated or archived dark web forums) to prove the AI, Graph, and Scanning logic works perfectly. 

# **2. Potential Challenges and Risks** 

- **Risk 1: Live Scraping Failures & Network Blocks (High Probability, High Impact)** Hackathon Wi-Fi networks often block Tor traffic. Furthermore, live Dark Web sites are slow, frequently go offline, and use aggressive anti-bot CAPTCHAs, which could cause a live demo to crash. 

- **Risk 2: AI False Positives (Adversarial Stylometry)** If a threat actor intentionally uses translation software or changes their typing style (adding fake typos), the AI model might fail to match them or incorrectly link two innocent profiles together. 

- **Risk 3: "Hairball" Graph Visualization** If the scraper pulls 10,000 entities, displaying them all at once on the React frontend will cause the UI to freeze and look like an unreadable "hairball," defeating the purpose of visual intelligence. 

- **Risk 4: Malicious Data Ingestion (Security Risk)** Scraping hacker forums means downloading untrusted text. Hackers could embed cross-site scripting (XSS) payloads or SQL injections into their forum bios to attack the tools scraping them. 

# **3. Strategies for Overcoming These Challenges** 

- **Mitigation for Risk 1 (The Hybrid Demo Strategy):** We will build a **Hybrid Data Pipeline** . For the SIH presentation, the primary demo will run on a prepopulated Neo4j database using verified open-source historical datasets (e.g., archived forum dumps). This guarantees a fast, zero-fail offline presentation. We will keep the live scraper script as a separate module to show judges the code works, but we won't rely on it for the main UI workflow. 

- **Mitigation for Risk 2 (Analyst-in-the-Loop AI):** The system will never make an automated arrest decision. The AI will strictly output a **"Confidence** 

**Score" (e.g., 87% Match)** . The UI will highlight the specific linguistic similarities (like unique slang or punctuation patterns) so the human intelligence analyst can make the final verification. 

- **Mitigation for Risk 3 (Smart UI Filtering):** The frontend (using Cytoscape.js or D3) will load nodes dynamically. We will implement strict UI filters (e.g., "Show connections up to 2 degrees of separation only," or "Filter by Date/Crypto Wallet"). This keeps the graph clean, fast, and readable. 

- **Mitigation for Risk 4 (Zero-Trust Architecture):** We will use strict data sanitization (stripping all HTML/executable code) before any scraped text touches the PostgreSQL or Neo4j databases. Additionally, the web scrapers will run inside isolated **Docker containers** without root privileges, preventing any reverse-attacks from compromising the host machine. 

Sabse pehle ek cybersecurity reality check: "100% uncrackable" jaisi koi cheez nahi hoti. Lekin hum is system ko itna secure zarur bana sakte hain ki duniya ke best hackers ke liye bhi isme ghusna practically impossible ho jaye. Is approach ko "Defense in Depth" (Multi-layered security) kehte hain. 

Kyunki aapka system seedha Dark Web hackers ke data ko scrape aur process karega, aapka threat model normal web apps se bahut alag aur dangerous hai. Apne system ki security maximize karne ke liye aapko in 5 layers par kaam karna hoga: 

1. OpSec (Operational Security) — Scraper ki Identity Chupana 

Hackers dark web forums par traps (honeytokens) lagate hain taaki unhe scrape karne walon ka real IP address pata chal jaye. 

Proxy Chaining: Aapka scraper kabhi bhi seedha internet se connect nahi hona chahiye. Hamesha Tor network aur multiple proxy layers (rotating proxies) ke through traffic bhejen. 

DNS Leak Protection: Ensure karein ki aapke scrapers Tor ka hi DNS use kar rahe hain, warna ISP ko pata chal jayega ki aapka server dark web access kar raha hai. 

Headless Browser Hardening: Agar aap Selenium/Puppeteer use kar rahe hain, toh uske "webdriver" flags hide karein, warna target site detect kar legi ki ye ek bot hai. 

# 2. Data Sanitization (The "Poisoned Data" Defense) 

Ye sabse critical point hai. Aap jin hackers ko track kar rahe hain, wo apne forum posts ya usernames mein malicious code (SQL Injection, XSS payloads, ya Zip bombs) likh kar chhod sakte hain. 

Strict Input Validation: Jab aapka scraper dark web se text uthaye, toh use seedha database mein save na karein. Us text ko sanitize karein (HTML tags strip karein, special characters escape karein). 

Zero-Trust Parsing: Agar system dark web se koi image ya file (jaise SSL cert) download kar raha hai, toh use execute hone ki permission kabhi na dein. Use isolated environment mein parse karein. 

# 3. Infrastructure & Deployment Security 

Aapka code kahan run ho raha hai, ye bahut matter karta hai. 

Docker Container Isolation: Har component (Scraper, Database, AI Model, Frontend) alag-alag Docker containers mein hona chahiye. Agar hacker galti se Scraper ko hack kar bhi le, toh wo Database tak nahi pahunch payega kyunki containers isolated hain. 

Air-Gapped Capability: NTRO jaisi agencies ke liye, aapka architecture aisa hona chahiye jo internet se completely disconnect hokar (Air-gapped mode mein) local server par run kar sake. 

# 4. Database & Data Security (At Rest & In Transit) 

Intelligence data highly classified hota hai. 

AES-256 Encryption: Aapka Neo4j (Graph) aur PostgreSQL database hard drive par encrypted hona chahiye. 

TLS 1.3: Frontend (React) aur Backend (FastAPI) ke beech jitna bhi data travel kare, wo end-to-end encrypted hona chahiye. 

Environment Variables: API keys (jaise Shodan ki key) ya database passwords kabhi bhi code/GitHub mein hardcode nahi hone chahiye. Inhe .env files ya AWS Secrets Manager jaisi jagah store karein. 

# 5. Access Control (IAM - Identity & Access Management) 

Agar system hack nahi ho sakta, toh hackers authorized user ka account churane ki koshish karenge. 

Strict Role-Based Access Control (RBAC): Har user ko sirf utna hi access dein jitni uski zarurat hai. Ek 'Junior Analyst' database delete nahi kar paana chahiye. 

Mandatory 2FA/MFA: Bina OTP ya hardware token (YubiKey) ke kisi bhi analyst ko dashboard par login na karne dein. 

Audit Logging: Backend mein ek log maintain karein ki "Kis user ne, kis IP se, kitne baje, konsa threat actor search kiya". Agar koi insider threat (gaddar) data churanne ki koshish kare, toh log mein pakda jayega.

security mai itne hi hai n ya or kuch or imp hai jo hum kar skatein hain bea cue automation, trigger hai jo aapne app detect karega 

Aapne bahut hi brilliant point pakda hai! Normal web apps ke liye wo 5 layers kaafi hain, lekin kyunki aapka system **automated triggers** par kaam karta hai (jaise hi naya data aaya, system automatically AI run karega ya nayi link scan karega), ye ek naya security risk paida karta hai. 

Jab system mein automation hota hai, toh hackers us automation ka hi fayda uthakar aapke system par attack kar sakte hain. Isko counter karne ke liye aapko **Automation & Trigger Security** (The 6th Layer) add karni padegi: 

# **6. Automation & Trigger Security (Guarding the Bots)** 

# **A. SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery) Protection** 

- **Khatra (Threat):** Jab aapka automated scanner kisi dark web forum par naya .onion link dekhta hai, toh wo use scan karne jata hai. Agar hacker ne jaanbujh kar .onion link ki jagah koi internal network ka IP (jaise 127.0.0.1 ya AWS ka internal metadata URL 169.254.169.254) hide karke daal diya, toh aapka scanner aapke hi server ki internal files ya API keys read karke hacker ko bhej sakta hai. 

- **Defense:** Aapke scanner mein **Strict URL/IP Validation** honi chahiye. Uska network rule aisa set karein ki wo sirf external internet/Tor par request bhej sake, internal IP addresses par request bhejna block (deny) ho. 

# **B. Resource Exhaustion (DDoS via Triggers)** 

- **Khatra (Threat):** AI stylometry model run karne mein GPU/CPU power lagti hai. Agar hackers samajh gaye ki aapka system har naye post par AI run karta hai, toh wo ek bot laga kar forum par 10,000 lambe-lambe garbage posts daal denge. Aapka trigger 10,000 baar AI model run karega, jisse aapka server overload hokar crash ho jayega (Denial of Service) aur cloud ka bill lakho mein aa jayega. 

- **Defense (Circuit Breaker & Queues):** Automated triggers ko seedha AI engine se connect na karein. Beech mein ek **Message Queue (jaise RabbitMQ ya Apache Kafka)** lagayen. Rate limiting set karein ki system 1 minute mein sirf 50 AI queries hi process karega. Agar limit cross hoti hai, toh "Circuit Breaker" pattern trigger ho jaye aur naye requests queue mein wait karein. 

# **C. Adversarial AI attacks (Model Poisoning)** 

- **Khatra (Threat):** Hackers aise paragraphs generate karke post kar sakte hain jisme hidden characters ya aisi language ho jo jaan-bujh kar NLP (Stylometry) model ko confuse karde ya use galat result (False Positive) dene par majboor karde. 

- **Defense:** AI engine trigger hone se pehle data ka **Length and Type Check** hona chahiye. Example: Agar text 5 words se chota hai, ya 10,000 words se bada hai, toh automation trigger hi na ho (Drop the request). AI ko ek threshold confidence (e.g., >75%) ke baad hi alert generate karne ki permission dein. 

# **D. Infinite Loop Prevention** 

- **Khatra (Threat):** Agar do automated systems aapas mein trigger ho gaye (e.g., User A ka link User B ko trigger kar raha hai aur User B ka wapas User A ko), toh system infinite loop mein phans jayega. 

- **Defense:** Har automated task ke paas ek **TTL (Time to Live)** aur **Max Retry limit** (jaise max 3 retries) honi chahiye. Agar koi scan 3 baar fail ho, toh trigger us task ko 'Dead Letter Queue' mein daal de aur aage badh jaye. 

**SIH Presentation mein ise kaise bole?** Pichle 5 points ke sath isko aise frame karein: "Kyunki humara system automated hai, hamara sabse bada risk hai SSRF aur Resource Exhaustion. Hackers hamare hi scanners ko overload karke server crash kar sakte hain. Isliye humne triggers ke aage Rate-limiting queues aur Strict Egress Filtering lagayi hai." 

Ye level ki security thinking (Automated Threat Modeling) ek average college team nahi karti. Ye definitely judges ko convince kar dega ki aapka architecture production-ready hai. 

or kuch securtiy 

Agar aap sach mein NTRO (Intelligence Agency) ke judges ko poori tarah impress karna chahte hain, toh ab hum **Advanced / Intelligence-Grade Security** ki baat karte hain. Ye wo techniques hain jo normal developers nahi sochte, lekin cyberdefense agencies (like NSA, NTRO) daily use karti hain. 

Pichle 6 points ke alawa, aap in **3 Elite Security Measures** ko add kar sakte hain: 

# **7. Active Defense (Hackers ko Trap karna - Honeytokens)** 

Abhi tak hum sirf bachne (defense) ki baat kar rahe the. Ab hum ulta hackers ko trap karenge. 

   - **Concept:** Aapke system ka dashboard aur code base toh secure hai, lekin aap jaan-bujh kar apne frontend code (React) ya network mein kuch "Fake API Keys" ya "Fake Admin URLs" (jaise /api/v1/admin-override-auth) chhupa denge. 

   - **Fayda:** Ek normal user kabhi us hidden link ya key ko access nahi karega. Lekin agar koi hacker aapke system par attack kar raha hai, toh wo sabse pehle un keys ko try karega. Jaise hi wo us fake link par click karega ya key use karega, aapka system us hacker ka IP address aur fingerprint silently record kar lega aur admin ko **High Priority Alert** bhej dega ki "System is under attack". 

   - SIH Flex: Isko **Canary Tokens** ya **Honeytokens** kehte hain. Judges ko bolna: "We are not just defending, we have planted honeytokens to identify internal or external attackers proactively." 

**8. Data Integrity & Chain of Custody (Legal Evidence Security)** 

Aapka system dark web se evidence (saboot) nikal raha hai. Kal ko agar police kisi ko court mein pesh karegi, toh criminal ka lawyer bol sakta hai ki "Ye database toh fake hai, kisi analyst ne manually entry add kardi hogi!" 

- **Concept:** Jaise hi scraper dark web se koi post ya image scrape kare, us raw data ka turant ek **SHA-256 Hash (Digital Fingerprint)** create karein aur use database mein save kar dein. 

- **Fayda:** Agar database mein kisi ne ek 'comma' (,) bhi change kiya, toh hash badal jayega. Ye prove karta hai ki jo data aapne dark web se uthaya tha, wo 100% original hai aur kisi ne uske sath ched-chad (tampering) nahi ki hai. Law enforcement ke liye isse **"Chain of Custody"** kehte hain. Ye forensic investigation ki sabse badi requirement hai. 

# **9. API Security (IDOR & BOLA Prevention)** 

Kyunki aap React (Frontend) aur FastAPI (Backend) use karenge, aapka backend data APIs ke through bhejega. 

- **Khatra (IDOR - Insecure Direct Object Reference):** Maan lijiye aapke system mein 2 analysts hain. Analyst 'A' API call karta hai GET /api/investigation/12 dekhne ke liye. Agar wo '12' ko change karke '13' kar de, aur use Analyst 'B' ki top-secret investigation file dikh jaye, toh ye bahut bada security flaw hai. 

- **Defense:** Har API endpoint par **Object-Level Authorization (BOLA prevention)** lagayen. Server ko check karna chahiye ki kya current user (JWT token) ko us specific record number '13' ko dekhne ka permission (RBAC clearance) hai ya nahi. Intelligence agencies mein data compartmentalization (Need-to-Know basis) bahut strict hota hai. 

**Isko Presentation mein kaise include karein? (The Ultimate Slide)** 

Aap apni PPT mein ek single slide banayen jiska title ho: **"Military-Grade Security & Forensics Architecture"** 

Usme ye 4 points likhein: 

1. **OpSec & Isolation:** 100% Containerized microservices with outbound-only proxy chaining to prevent IP leaks. 

2. **Anti-Automation Abuse:** RabbitMQ queuing + Rate Limiting to prevent SSRF and algorithmic DDoS attacks. 

3. **Forensic Integrity:** SHA-256 cryptographic hashing of all scraped raw data to maintain a legal "Chain of Custody". 

4. **Active Defense (Deception):** Embedded Honeytokens in the UI to instantly detect and trap unauthorized insider threats or hackers.

SIH PROBLEM STATEMENT 

Problem Statement ID26151 

Problem Statement TitleDark web threat actor de-anonymization 

Description• Background The dark web has become a preferred operating space for threat actors in the modern age, mainly because it lets them hide their identity behind Tor hidden services, which makes attribution of threat actors operating on darkweb the main challenge for any investigation. Such threat actors carry out a wide range of unlawful activities such as drugs and arms sale, stolen data and hacking services, money laundering, terror financing, etc. The objective of this problem statement is to build a system for the deanonymization of dark web threat actors and link them to suspect real-world entities. 

• Description The system shall deanonymize dark web threat actors by continuously gathering their footprints from a range of sources (marketplaces, forums, deep web etc.) and linking them to the identifying information available on those sources. The system envisages three core capabilities. First, finding misconfigurations in Tor hidden servicesâ€”such as exposed server-status pages, SSL certificates tied to clearnet domains, default service banners, descriptor inconsistencies, etc and matching them with clearnet infrastructure to point to the likely origin servers. Second, mapping threat actors across multiple marketplaces into a single relationship graph of handles, PGP keys, wallets and trust links. Third, using AIbased analysis, including stylometric persona identification and behavioural profiling, to link rebranded or migrated personas to known threat actors. The system shall provide an analytical front end to query the database across a chosen timeline and shall work in an autonomous mode, drawing on available sources of good quality and reliability. 

• Expected Solution An end-to-end system shall be developed for the collection, storage, contextualization and querying (through GUI/dashboards) of dark web threat actor intelligenceâ€”covering actor profiles, identifiers (handles, PGP keys, wallets etc.), hidden service infrastructure indicators, persona linkages, attribution confidence, category, last scan date and source. The system shall also provide the facility to export the result set in CSV, JSON and report formats. 

OrganizationNational Technical Research Organisation (NTRO)DepartmentNational Technical Research Organisation (NTRO)CategorySoftwareThemeBlockchain & CybersecurityYoutube LinkDataset LinkContact info 

Here is the deep, evidence-based problem-to-solution analysis for the selected SIH Problem Statement. 

1. EXACT PROBLEM STATEMENT 

PS ID 

[26151] 

Exact Problem Statement 

# Dark web threat actor de-anonymization 

• Background: The dark web has become a preferred operating space for threat actors in the modern age, mainly because it lets them hide their identity behind Tor hidden services, which makes attribution of threat actors operating on darkweb the main challenge for any investigation. Such threat actors carry out a wide range of unlawful activities such as drugs and arms sale, stolen data and hacking services, money laundering, terror financing, etc. The objective of this problem statement is to build a system for the deanonymization of dark web threat actors and link them to suspect real-world entities. 

• Description: The system shall deanonymize dark web threat actors by continuously gathering their footprints from a range of sources (marketplaces, forums, deep web etc.) and linking them to the identifying information available on those sources. The system envisages three core capabilities. First, finding misconfigurations in Tor hidden services—such as exposed server-status pages, SSL certificates tied to clearnet domains, default service banners, descriptor inconsistencies, etc and matching them with clearnet infrastructure to point to the likely origin servers. Second, mapping threat actors across multiple marketplaces into a single relationship graph of handles, PGP keys, wallets and trust links. Third, using AIbased analysis, including stylometric persona identification and behavioural profiling, to link rebranded or migrated personas to known threat actors. The system shall provide an analytical front end to query the database across a chosen timeline and shall work in an autonomous mode, drawing on available sources of good quality and reliability. 

• Expected Solution: An end-to-end system shall be developed for the collection, storage, contextualization and querying (through GUI/dashboards) of dark web threat actor intelligence—covering actor profiles, identifiers (handles, PGP keys, wallets etc.), hidden service infrastructure indicators, persona linkages, attribution confidence, category, last scan date and source. The system shall also provide the facility to export the result set in CSV, JSON and report formats. 

Answer: 

What is the PS actually asking us to solve? NTRO wants a centralized intelligence platform (a unified OSINT/threat-intel tool) that scrapes the Dark Web (Tor), analyzes technical mistakes made by server admins, tracks cryptocurrency and PGP footprints, and uses AI to analyze writing styles. The goal is to unmask anonymous criminals and connect their different fake identities to each other and eventually to their real-world identities. 

What does each important sentence mean? 

Continuous gathering: Needs automated web scrapers routed through Tor. 

Misconfigurations: Finding technical flaws (like a server accidentally revealing its real IP address or using a public SSL certificate on a hidden service) to locate the physical server. 

Mapping actors: Using Graph databases to link a user on Market A to a user on Market B because they used the same Bitcoin wallet or PGP encryption key. 

AI-based stylometric analysis: Using NLP to prove "HackerX" is the same person as "VendorY" based on how they type, spell, and use grammar. 

What is the actual problem behind the wording? Law enforcement currently does these steps manually or uses highly fragmented, expensive tools. There is no single open/custom platform that combines infrastructure scanning, graph mapping, and AI linguistics specifically tailored for Indian intelligence agencies. 

Why does this problem exist? Tor is designed to make tracing impossible by bouncing traffic. Criminals use Tor to operate with impunity. 

Who is facing this problem? Intelligence agencies (NTRO, RAW, IB), cyber police, and national security organizations. 

Who is responsible for solving it today? Cyber threat intelligence analysts, OSINT researchers, and specialized law enforcement units. 

What happens if this problem remains unsolved? Threat actors continue to sell drugs, weapons, and stolen national data without fear of arrest. 

What outcome does the organization actually want? A dashboard where an analyst can type a username like "DarkLord" and instantly see their connected Bitcoin wallets, their other usernames across 5 different forums, the real IP address of their hidden server (if misconfigured), and a confidence score that they are the same person. 

What would a successful solution look like? An automated backend engine doing continuous Tor crawling, a Neo4j (or similar) graph database connecting the dots, an AI model scoring writing styles, and a React/Angular frontend displaying intelligence graphs. 

Findings: 

A. Explicitly stated by the PS: Must use AI stylometry, must build a relationship graph (PGP/Wallets/Handles), must scan for Tor misconfigurations (SSL/Server-status), must export to CSV/JSON. 

B. Reasonable inference: The system requires managing Tor proxies to avoid bans, requires a graph database, and needs integration with clearnet datasets (like Shodan/Censys) to match SSL certificates. 

C. Things that need further research/verification: How to continuously scrape dark web marketplaces without getting blocked by their anti-bot protections (captchas, login walls). 

# 2. REAL-WORLD PROBLEM 

What is happening today? Threat actors operate on Dark Web forums (like Exploit, XSS, or former markets like AlphaBay/Silk Road equivalents). They frequently change usernames (rebranding) when a market is shut down by police.Who experiences the problem? Intelligence analysts who have to manually read thousands of forum posts to figure out if a new threat actor is actually an old, known criminal.How frequently does it happen? Daily. The Dark Web ecosystem is highly volatile; markets close and open constantly, causing mass migrations of users.Why is it difficult? The Dark Web has no central search engine. Sites go offline randomly. Threat actors use operational security (OpSec) to hide.What causes it? The cryptographic routing of the Tor network hides IP addresses, and cryptocurrencies pseudo-anonymize finances.What are the consequences? Delayed investigations, unpunished cybercrimes, and national security threats.What resources are currently wasted? Thousands of human man-hours spent manually tracking PGP keys, comparing forum posts, and running individual Python scripts to check server status.Where do delays occur? Manually correlating a Bitcoin wallet found on a Dark Web forum with a clearnet exchange.Where do errors occur? Assuming two actors are different people because they use different usernames.Where is human intervention required? Connecting technical evidence (IPs/Certs) to behavioral evidence (writing style).Where does data become unavailable, duplicated, outdated, or incorrect? Dark web sites frequently undergo DDoS attacks or change onion addresses, making static links dead. 

# Simple Example: 

A hacker named "Shadow99" sells stolen Indian credit cards on Dark Market A. Market A gets seized by the FBI. Two weeks later, a new user named "NightRider" appears on Market B selling similar credit cards. 

Currently, an analyst has to manually check if NightRider uses the same PGP key or Bitcoin wallet as Shadow99. If they don't, the trail goes cold.With our system: The AI reads NightRider's posts, notices he uses the exact same rare grammatical errors and slang as Shadow99. The system also notices NightRider's Tor server accidentally exposed an SSL certificate that maps to a real IP address in Eastern Europe. The analyst is instantly notified. 

# 3. PROBLEM DECOMPOSITION 

Main Problem: De-anonymizing Dark Web threat actors and attributing them to realworld entities.→ Sub-problem 1: Data Collection in a Hostile Environment 

What causes it: Dark web sites use CAPTCHAs, require logins, and block automated scrapers. 

Current limitation: Standard scrapers fail on Tor. 

Technology: Tor proxy rotation, headless browsers, CAPTCHA solving. 

→ Sub-problem 2: Finding Tor Infrastructure Misconfigurations 

What causes it: Lazy server admins configure Apache/Nginx poorly, leaking their real server IP. 

Current solution: Manual tools like Nmap, manual Shodan searches. 

Technology: Automated banner grabbing, SSL certificate parsing, Shodan API integration. 

→ Sub-problem 3: Identity Fragmentation (Graph Mapping) 

What causes it: Criminals use different usernames across different sites. 

Current limitation: Analysts use manual spreadsheets or paid tools like Maltego to draw links. 

Technology: Graph databases (Neo4j), Entity Resolution algorithms. 

→ Sub-problem 4: Persona Rebranding (Stylometry) 

What causes it: Criminals change their names and cryptographic keys to start fresh. Current limitation: Very hard to track without human linguistic analysis. 

Technology: Natural Language Processing (NLP), Transformer models (BERT) for stylometric embeddings. 

CORE PROBLEM: 

Existing intelligence tools are either entirely manual, highly fragmented, or prohibitively expensive, meaning analysts cannot automatically and continuously correlate technical server flaws, financial footprints, and behavioral linguistics into a single, actionable attribution graph. 

4. CURRENT SYSTEM / CURRENT PROCESS 

Problem occurs: A new cyberattack occurs, and data is posted on a Dark Web forum. ↓Who receives the problem? NTRO / CERT-In / Cyber Police analysts. 

↓What happens next? Analysts boot up an isolated VM, connect to Tor, and manually browse the forum. 

↓What data is collected? They copy-paste the threat actor's username, PGP key, Bitcoin address, and post content into a local text file or spreadsheet. 

↓Which system/tool is used? Tor Browser, Excel, Maltego (manual entry), Python scripts for scraping. 

↓Who makes the decision? The human analyst manually cross-references the PGP key with open PGP servers. 

↓What action is taken? The analyst tries to find a clearnet IP using tools like Shodan. ↓What is the final outcome? A PDF intelligence report is generated days or weeks later. 

Major Bottlenecks: 

Manual Scraping: Tor is slow; manual scraping is impossible to scale. 

Siloed Analysis: Investigating server IPs (Infrastructure) and investigating user behavior (Stylometry) are currently done by completely different teams using different tools. 

No Continuous Monitoring: If a server is misconfigured for just 5 minutes, a manual analyst will miss it. An automated system will catch it.

Building a dark web deanonymization platform requires bridging cybersecurity, data engineering, and artificial intelligence. You do not need to be an elite penetration tester to build this, but you do need to understand how web infrastructure works and where criminals make technical mistakes. 

Here is the sequential learning path to take your team from absolute beginners to building a working prototype. 

1. Networking & OSINT (Open Source Intelligence) 

Internet Infrastructure: Learn how TCP/IP, DNS, and HTTP/HTTPS function. You must understand how a normal website connects to a user before you can understand how the dark web hides those connections. 

The Tor Protocol: Study Onion Routing. Learn what .onion hidden services are, how Tor nodes encrypt traffic, and the difference between the deep web and the dark web. 

Server Misconfigurations: Understand how web servers (Apache, Nginx) operate. Learn how simple administrative mistakes—like leaving a /server-status page public, exposing an .env file, or reusing a public SSL certificate—leak the real IP address of a hidden server. 

OSINT Tools: Learn to use Shodan and Censys. These are search engines for internet-connected devices. You need to know how to query them via API to match leaked SSL certificates to physical server locations. 

2. Python & Automated Data Collection 

Advanced Python: Python is the industry standard for both threat intelligence and AI. Your team needs strong foundational Python skills. 

Regex (Regular Expressions): Learn to write patterns that automatically scan raw HTML and extract specific data formats, such as Bitcoin wallet addresses, PGP encryption keys, and email addresses. 

Web Scraping: Master libraries like Beautiful Soup and Scrapy to automatically extract text and links from web pages. 

Proxy Routing: Learn how to route your Python scrapers through Tor proxies (like Privoxy). If your scrapers connect directly to the clear web, you cannot access .onion sites. 

# 3. Graph Databases 

Graph Theory Basics: Understand the concept of Nodes (entities like usernames, IPs, and crypto wallets) and Edges (the relationships connecting them, such as "hosted on" or "transacted with"). 

Neo4j & Cypher: Learn Neo4j, the leading graph database, and its query language, Cypher. Standard SQL databases are terrible at relationship mapping; Neo4j is built specifically to connect the dots between fragmented identities. 

4. Artificial Intelligence & Stylometry 

NLP (Natural Language Processing): Learn how computers process human text using tokenization and word embeddings. 

Stylometry: Study how algorithms identify an author based on their writing behavior (e.g., punctuation frequency, unique vocabulary, grammatical errors). 

Deep Learning Frameworks: Get comfortable with PyTorch and the Hugging Face Transformers library. 

Transformer Models: Learn how to fine-tune pre-trained models (like BERT or RoBERTa) for binary classification so the AI can look at a post from "User A" and a post from "User B" and output a probability score that they are the same person. 

5. Full-Stack Development 

Backend APIs: Learn FastAPI (Python) to build the bridge that allows your frontend to query the Neo4j database and trigger the AI model. 

Frontend Framework: Learn React.js to build the intelligence dashboard. 

Graph Visualization: Learn libraries like react-force-graph or Cytoscape.js to render the Neo4j data as an interactive, clickable web of connected threats for the user interface.

Here are the core concepts and terms you need to know, grouped by theme and explained in plain English without jargon. 

# 1. The Dark Web & Tor Ecosystem 

Clearnet: The everyday internet you use (Google, YouTube, Instagram). Search engines can index it, and every device connected to it has a visible, trackable public IP address. 

Dark Web: A small subsection of the internet that cannot be accessed through standard browsers like Chrome. It requires specialized software to access, and the websites are intentionally hidden to keep visitors and server owners anonymous. 

Tor (The Onion Router): Free, open-source software and network designed to provide online anonymity. When you browse using Tor, your traffic is encrypted in multiple layers (like an onion) and bounced through three random computers (nodes/relays) worldwide before reaching the destination. 

Hidden Service (.onion site): A website hosted inside the Tor network instead of the regular internet. It does not use standard domain names like .com or .in; instead, it has a long string of random letters and numbers ending in .onion (e.g., expyuzz5wqqfdgah56...onion). The website’s physical server location and IP address remain hidden. 

Tor Exit Node: The third and final computer in the Tor chain that delivers traffic to the destination. While hidden services keep traffic inside the Tor network, exit nodes matter when someone inside Tor accesses a regular clearnet website. 

# 2. Digital Clues & Identifiers 

Handle: The online username or pseudonym a threat actor chooses on a forum or marketplace (e.g., "DarkLord99" or "GhostRider"). 

OpSec (Operational Security): The habits and practices people use to protect sensitive or secret information. When a criminal forgets to turn on their VPN, reuses an old password, or uses the same nickname across two platforms, they commit an OpSec failure—which is how investigators catch them. 

Digital Footprint: The trail of data left behind when someone uses the internet. On the dark web, this includes forum posts, upload times, public keys, and wallet addresses. 

PGP Key (Pretty Good Privacy): A cryptographic system used on dark web forums to verify identity and encrypt messages. A threat actor publishes a Public Key so anyone can send them encrypted messages or verify that a post actually came from them. Because PGP keys are unique, if "HackerA" and "VendorB" publish the same PGP key, they are guaranteed to be the same entity. 

Cryptocurrency Wallet Address: A string of letters and numbers (like an account number) used to send and receive digital currencies (Bitcoin, Monero). Bitcoin's ledger is public, meaning every transaction to and from that address is visible to everyone forever. 

3. Server Flaws & Infrastructure 

IP Address (Internet Protocol Address): The unique digital street address assigned to any internet-connected device or server. Finding a threat actor's real-world IP address reveals their physical location or hosting provider. 

Server Misconfiguration: An error made by a website administrator when setting up their server software (like Apache or Nginx). For example, leaving default diagnostic pages open or forgetting to turn off features that broadcast the server's real IP address to the public. 

Exposed server-status Page: A built-in Apache web server diagnostic page that displays server performance metrics and active web connections. If left publicly accessible on a dark web server, an investigator can view the real IP addresses communicating with that server. 

SSL/TLS Certificate: A digital certificate that authenticates a website’s identity and enables encrypted HTTPS connections. If a criminal uses the exact same SSL certificate on both their secret .onion site and their public clearnet website, they have linked their hidden service directly to a real IP address. 

Banner Grabbing: A reconnaissance technique where a scanner connects to a server and asks for basic info. The server responds with a "banner"—revealing its operating system, server version, and default software tags. 

Shodan / Censys: Search engines for internet-connected devices (servers, webcams, routers). Instead of searching web page text like Google, they scan the entire internet 24/7 for open ports, SSL certificates, and server banners. 

# 4. Investigation & Data Concepts 

De-anonymization: The process of stripping away layers of anonymity to link a digital pseudonym, hidden server, or anonymous account to a real-world person, company, or physical computer. 

Attribution: Formally proving who committed an action. Attribution answers: "Which specific group or individual operated handle X and set up server Y?" 

OSINT (Open Source Intelligence): Gathering, analyzing, and correlating publicly accessible information (forums, public registries, open key servers, social platforms) to produce actionable intelligence. 

Graph Database: A database that stores information as Nodes (objects like a Person, Wallet, or IP) and Edges (the relationships connecting them, such as OWNS, TRANSFERS_TO, or POSTS_FROM). It is designed to quickly answer questions like: "Show me every username connected to this specific Bitcoin wallet within 3 hops." 

Entity Resolution: The algorithmic process of determining whether two different online records (e.g., user "Shadow" on Forum 1 and user "Night" on Forum 2) actually refer to the same real-world individual. 

# 5. AI & Behavioral Analysis 

Stylometry: The study of linguistic style. Everyone has distinct writing habits—the specific punctuation they prefer, words they misspell, average sentence lengths, and slang they use. Stylometric algorithms analyze these patterns mathematically. 

Persona Rebranding: When a criminal abandons an identity (often because a marketplace was seized by police) and creates a brand-new username on another platform to start fresh. 

NLP (Natural Language Processing): The subfield of artificial intelligence focused on helping computers understand, interpret, and manipulate human language. 

Text Embeddings: Converting a block of text into a list of numbers (a mathematical vector) that captures its semantic meaning and writing style. Computers cannot read words, but they can compare two vectors to see how close they are in mathematical space. 

Similarity Score / Confidence Score: A percentage or probability (e.g., 0.87 or 87%) generated by an AI model indicating how likely it is that two pieces of text were written by the same human being.

This is a highly effective team composition for this specific problem statement. Because this project requires heavy data processing, complex visualizations, and specialized machine learning, having a clear division of labor is what will keep your team moving fast. 

Since your team already has experience tackling hackathons with custom machine learning models, you can apply that same integration mindset here. For anyone in the group aiming to transition their skills toward an AI engineering role, this project provides a massive opportunity to work on applied NLP. 

Here is exactly how you should divide the responsibilities to build the prototype. 

The AI / ML Team (2 Persons) 

This duo is responsible for proving that two different usernames belong to the same person based on how they write. 

AI Developer 1 (The NLP Architect): This person focuses entirely on the Stylometry Model. Their job is to take an open-source dataset of forum posts, clean it, and finetune a Transformer model (like RoBERTa) for authorship verification. They need to build a model that takes two paragraphs of text and outputs a similarity percentage. 

AI Developer 2 (Data & ML Integrator): Models are useless without clean data pipelines. This person handles the Entity Extraction and API wrapping. They write the 

logic (using NLP libraries like spaCy or complex Regex) to automatically spot and extract PGP keys, emails, and Bitcoin wallets from raw text. They also wrap the Stylometry Model in a Python API so the backend can easily send it text to analyze. 

The Full Stack Team (2 Persons) 

This duo builds the actual application that the judges will see and use. 

Full Stack Developer 1 (Backend & Graph Architect): Standard SQL databases will fail at this task, so this developer needs to take ownership of Neo4j (the graph database) and Python FastAPI. Their job is to receive data from the scrapers, structure it into Nodes and Edges, and write the Cypher queries that find connections (e.g., "Find all users connected to this Bitcoin wallet"). 

Full Stack Developer 2 (Frontend & UI Visualization): Relying on a solid foundation of HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, this developer will build the React.js dashboard. Their most critical task is mastering a graph visualization library like react-forcegraph or Cytoscape.js. The entire success of the demo rests on this person's ability to make the threat data look like a professional, interactive intelligence tool. 

The Cybersecurity / OSINT Lead (1 Person) 

This single role is the engine of the project. While the rest of the team builds the analysis platform, this person gathers the raw materials. 

The Cyber/Infrastructure Lead: This person does not need to build the UI or the AI. Their sole focus is writing the Python scripts that securely connect to Tor (using proxies) to scrape dark web forums. Crucially, they are also responsible for building the Misconfiguration Scanner—the script that checks a .onion address for exposed SSL certificates and queries the Shodan API to find its real-world IP address. 

How the Team Integrates (The Workflow) 

To avoid blocking each other during the first few weeks, you should work in parallel using simulated data: 

Cybersecurity downloads an offline dataset of archived forum posts and hands it to the team so no one has to wait for live Tor scrapers to be built. 

AI/ML uses that offline dataset to train the stylometry model and write the extraction scripts. 

Full Stack uses the same offline dataset to populate a local Neo4j database and build the visual UI around it. 

Once all three standalone pieces work, the team connects them together into one live pipeline.

As the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Lead for this project, you are the engine. The AI and Full Stack teams cannot do their jobs until you successfully and safely extract data from the Dark Web and map .onion hidden services back to real-world IP addresses. 

Your role does not require you to be a master hacker or penetration tester. Instead, you are an OSINT (Open-Source Intelligence) engineer. 

Here is your detailed, step-by-step roadmap to go from absolute beginner to building a working SIH prototype. 

Phase 1: Setup and Operational Security (OpSec) 

Goal: Build a safe environment so you can interact with the dark web without accidentally leaking your own IP address or getting hacked. 

What to learn: 

Virtualization: Learn how to use VirtualBox or VMware. Never scrape the dark web from your main host OS. 

The Tor Network: Understand how Tor works (Entry nodes, Relays, Exit nodes). Understand what a v3 .onion address is (a 56-character hidden service address). 

Linux Fundamentals: Get comfortable with the Ubuntu or Debian command line. 

What to do: 

Build a Sandbox VM: Install a fresh Ubuntu Virtual Machine. Take a "Snapshot" so you can always revert it if something breaks. 

Install the Tor Daemon: Do not just install the "Tor Browser". You need the background Tor service running on Linux. Install tor (version 0.4.9+) and verify it is listening on port 9050 (the default SOCKS5 proxy port). 

Learn socks5h: Understand the difference between socks5 and socks5h. When writing code to talk to Tor, you MUST use socks5h so the Tor network handles the DNS resolution. If you use regular socks5, your local machine will try to resolve the .onion domain and fail. 

SIEMtune 

Phase 2: Building the Dark Web Scraper 

Goal: Write a Python script that can visit an .onion forum, bypass basic protections, and download the HTML text so your AI team can analyze it. 

What to learn: 

Python requests library: Learn how to route HTTP requests through a proxy. 

Python Stem library: This is the official Tor controller library for Python. It allows your Python script to talk to the Tor daemon to do things like request a "new identity" (change your IP address) if a dark web forum blocks your current connection. 

# SIEMtune 

HTML Parsing: Learn BeautifulSoup to extract text from messy website code. 

What to do: 

Write a Hello World Scraper: Write a Python script using requests that connects to socks5h://127.0.0.1:9050. Have it fetch a known, safe onion site (like the DuckDuckGo onion mirror) and print the HTML. 

Explore Existing Tools: Look at open-source dark web OSINT tools like TorBot (updated recently in 2026). Read their code to see how they handle crawling. Do not just copy it—understand it. 

# PyPI 

Generate a Synthetic Dataset (CRITICAL): Do not wait until you have a perfect dark web scraper to give data to your AI team. Go to the clear web and download an archived dataset of an old forum (like the AzSecure dark web dataset or old RaidForums dumps). Give this JSON/CSV file to your AI and Full Stack teammates immediately so they can start building the graph and AI model. 

Phase 3: The De-anonymization Engine (The Core Innovation) 

Goal: This is the heart of the SIH problem statement. You must build a script that finds technical mistakes made by criminals running hidden servers, and maps those mistakes to their real, physical IP addresses. 

What to learn: 

Server Misconfigurations: Read up on Apache mod_status (the /server-status page) and how it accidentally leaks active IP connections. 

SSL/TLS Certificates: Learn how HTTPS works. Understand that if a criminal uses the same SSL certificate for their secret .onion site and their public clearnet site, they can be tracked via the certificate's unique Serial Number or SHA-256 fingerprint. 

The Shodan API: Shodan is a search engine for servers. Learn how to use the shodan-python library. 

What to do: 

Build the onion_scanner.py script: Write a Python script that takes a target .onion URL and does the following: 

Banner Grabbing: Reads the HTTP response headers (e.g., Server: Apache/2.4.41 (Ubuntu)). 

SSL Extraction: Connects via HTTPS and downloads the SSL certificate, extracting the Serial Number. 

Endpoint Probing: Automatically checks if target.onion/server-status or target.onion/.env is accidentally left open. 

Integrate Shodan: Write a function that takes the SSL Serial Number you just found on the dark web and queries the Shodan API (e.g., ssl.cert.serial:<number>). If Shodan has seen that exact same certificate on the regular internet, Shodan will return the real IP address. You have just de-anonymized the server. 

Phase 4: Entity Extraction (Connecting the Graph) 

Goal: Extract the "clues" from the text you scraped so the Full Stack developer can put them into the Neo4j graph database. 

What to learn: 

Regex (Regular Expressions): The language of pattern matching. 

What to do: 

Write Python Regex functions to automatically scan thousands of forum posts and extract: 

Cryptocurrency Addresses: (e.g., Bitcoin addresses start with 1, 3, or bc1). 

PGP Public Keys: (Blocks of text starting with -----BEGIN PGP PUBLIC KEY BLOCK-----). 

Email addresses and Usernames. 

Package this data cleanly into JSON format and hand it over to the Full Stack developer to feed into their Neo4j database. 

Phase 5: Demo Preparation (How to Win) 

Goal: Ensure the presentation goes flawlessly without relying on the slow, unpredictable Tor network during a live hackathon. 

What to do: 

Simulate a Target: Because the live dark web is slow and hackathon Wi-Fi often blocks Tor, build a fake hidden service locally. 

Setup a local Nginx server on a VM, configure it as a hidden service, and purposely misconfigure it (give it a fake leaked SSL cert and an exposed /server-status page). 

During the demo, point your onion_scanner.py at this local test server. It will instantly execute the scan, find the fake flaw, and hit the Shodan API to "prove" it found the real IP address. 

Summary Checklist for You: 

- [ ] Setup an Ubuntu VM. 

- [ ] Install tor and verify port 9050 is open. 

- [ ] Write a Python script using requests + socks5h to fetch an onion page. 

- [ ] Give your team a static CSV of fake/archived forum data immediately. 

- [ ] Write Regex scripts to extract Bitcoin wallets and PGP keys from text. 

- [ ] Write the Scanner script to pull SSL certificates from onion sites. 

[ ] Create a free Shodan account and learn to query certificate serial numbers via their API. 

[ ] Build a local, purposely vulnerable "dummy" Tor server for a safe, high-speed live demo.

can we use proxy chain for this or we are using it already 

Nahi, abhi hum **Proxychains** use nahi kar rahe hain. Abhi humne jo setup kiya hai, use **Application-Level Proxying** kehte hain. 

Aapke sawaal ka detail mein jawab aur donon ke beech ka farq ye hai: 

**1. Hum abhi kya kar rahe hain? (Application-Level Proxy)** 

Humne apne Python script (requests library) ke andar manually define kiya hai ki "Tor ke port 9050 se connect ho jao". Iska matlab sirf hamara Python script Tor se ja raha hai, baaki pura Linux system normal internet use kar raha hai. 

- **Fayda:** Coding ke liye ye best aur sabse fast tarika hai. Production mein API deploy karte waqt ye kabhi crash nahi hota. 

# **2. Proxychains kya hai aur kya humein use karna chahiye?** 

**Proxychains** ek alag tool hai jo aapke OS level par kaam karta hai. Ye kisi bhi command ya software ko zabardasti Tor ke through bhej deta hai, chahe us software mein proxy ki setting ho ya na ho. 

- **Kya humein chahiye? YES!** Scraper ke liye hum Python wala tarika hi use karenge, lekin jab aap **Infrastructure Scanner** banayenge (jisme hume .onion sites par nmap ya curl chalana hoga misconfigurations dhoondhne ke liye), tab humein Proxychains ki zarurat padegi. 

**Chaliye aapke VM mein Proxychains setup kar lete hain:** 

Kyunki aap cybersecurity lead hain, aapke VM mein Proxychains hona hi chahiye. Ise install aur configure karne ke steps: 

**Step 1: Install karein** Terminal mein type karein: 

# Bash 

sudo apt-get install proxychains4 -y 

**Step 2: Proxychains ko Tor ke sath link karein** Hamein config file mein batana hoga ki traffic Tor (port 9050) se bhejo. Config file open karein: 

# Bash 

sudo nano /etc/proxychains4.conf 

- Ek file khulegi. Apne keyboard ke 'Down Arrow' se sabse niche (end mein) jayein. 

- Wahan aapko [ProxyList] likha dikhega. 

- Uske niche ye line add karein (agar pehle se socks4 127.0.0.1 9050 likha hai, toh use change karke socks5 kar dein): 

# Plaintext 

socks5  127.0.0.1 9050 

(Save karne ke liye Ctrl+O dabayein, phir Enter, aur bahar aane ke liye Ctrl+X dabayein). 

**Step 3: Test karein** Ab aap koi bhi command proxychains4 likh kar chalayenge, toh wo seedha Dark Web (Tor) se hote hue jayega. Check karne ke liye apna IP address dekhein: 

Bina proxychains ke (aapka real IP dikhega): 

Bash 

curl ifconfig.me 

Proxychains ke sath (Aapko Tor ka IP dikhega, yaani aapki identity hide ho gayi): 

Bash 

proxychains4 curl ifconfig.me 

Aapne bahut advanced concept point out kiya! As a Cybersecurity person, aapko clear hona chahiye: 

- **Python Scraper ke liye:** Hum code mein socks5h use karenge (jo humne kiya). 

- **External scanning/reconnaissance ke liye:** Hum terminal mein proxychains4 use karenge. 

Kya Proxychains ka IP test successful raha? Agar haan, toh ab hum apne Python Scraper ko likhna start karte hain!

Ye aam taur par tab hota hai jab Tor service ya toh band ho, ya usne abhi tak Tor network ke sath apna connection (bootstrapping) poora na kiya ho.

Is problem ko fix karne ke liye in steps ko follow karein: 

1. **Tor Service ko Restart karein:** Terminal mein ye command run karke Tor daemon ko fresh start dein:

2. **Tor ka Status Check karein:** Tor network se circuit banne mein 10-30 seconds lag sakte hain. Status check karein aur ensure karein ki wahan active (running) likha hai: 

# Bash

(Keyboard par 'q' press karke status screen se bahar aayein). 

3. **Dubara Test Karein:** Restart karne ke baad thoda wait karein aur wapas apna Proxychains test run karein: 

Bash 

proxychains4 curl ifconfig.me 

Agar is baar bhi timeout aaye, toh iska matlab Tor aapke network (ISP) dvara block ho sakta hai ya port bind nahi ho raha. Us case mein hume Tor ke logs dekhne padenge. Aap Tor logs check karne ke liye ye command run kar sakte hain: 

# Bash 

sudo journalctl -eu tor --no-pager | tail -n 20

Iske 2 main reasons hote hain: 

1. Tor service ne abhi tak duniya ke doosre nodes ke sath apne circuits (rasta) poore nahi kiye hain (isko "Bootstrapping" kehte hain). 

2. Aapke Kali VM ka Time/Date galat hai. (Tor network strict cryptography use karta hai, agar time thoda bhi aage-peeche hua, toh connection fail ho jata hai). 

Isko fix karne ke liye in steps ko follow karein: 

# **Step 1: Tor Service ko Restart karein** 

Terminal mein ye command daalein taaki Tor fresh circuits banaye: 

Bash 

sudo systemctl restart tor 

# **Step 2: 30-40 Seconds Wait karein** 

Restart karne ke baad, Tor ko duniya bhar ke nodes se connect hone mein thoda time lagta hai. Kam se kam 30 seconds wait karein. 

# **Step 3: Script Dubara Run karein** 

Wait karne ke baad script ko wapas run karein: 

# Bash 

python3 scraper.py 

**Agar iske baad bhi same error aaye:** Toh hume Tor ke internal logs dekhne padenge ki kahan block ho raha hai. Us case mein ye command run karke jo output aaye, wo mujhe bhejein: 

# Bash 

sudo journalctl -eu tor --no-pager | tail -n 20 

Pehle restart aur wait wala step try karke batayein! 

Screenshot mein jo logs dikh rahe hain, usme tor.service properly start aur stop ho rahi hai. Lekin Kali Linux mein tor.service sirf ek "master" service hoti hai. Asli connection ka kaam uske andar chalne wali tor@default service karti hai.
